findings.summary: Feedback is a process where a system's outputs are routed back as inputs to influence future status, forming a causal loop. It enables self-regulation by comparing actual performance against a reference level and adjusting accordingly. The mechanism can either amplify or dampen system behavior depending on the phase and path of the returned signal.

mechanisms.title: Negative feedback stabilization
mechanisms.explanation: Returns a signal out of phase by 180° to reduce system error, minimizing deviations from a target state such as speed or temperature. This mechanism narrows the gap between actual and reference values, promoting stability.

mechanisms.title: Positive feedback amplification
mechanisms.explanation: Returns a signal in phase with the input, reinforcing the original output and potentially amplifying disturbances, oscillations, or system gain until a limit or saturation point is reached.

unknowns: Exact physical or neural wiring required to represent feedback in complex biological systems
Whether all feedback loops require an explicit wire or nerve pathway to qualify as feedback
The precise conditions under which positive feedback transitions into instability or runaway amplification
How practical experimenters distinguish intentional feedback from incidental circular causality
